 The Cheapest Medicare Plan Could Cost You More: Three Things to Check Before December 7
 Published
 9 hours ago on
 November 7, 2026 
 By
 Royal Examiner 
 A Medicare plan with a $0 monthly premium sounds like a bargain.
 But what happens when you discover that one of your prescriptions costs considerably more, your favorite pharmacy isn’t preferred, or the doctor you’ve seen for years is no longer in the plan’s network?
 Suddenly, that inexpensive plan may not be such a good deal.
 With Medicare’s annual Open Enrollment Period underway, millions of Americans have until December 7, 2026 , to review their coverage and make changes for 2027.
 And one of the most important things to understand is that the monthly premium doesn’t tell the whole story.
 The real cost of a Medicare plan includes premiums, deductibles, prescription drug expenses, copayments, coinsurance, and what you may have to pay when visiting doctors or hospitals.
 A plan that looks inexpensive on paper can cost considerably more over the course of a year.
 Before choosing or renewing Medicare coverage, pay close attention to three checks.
 Check Your Prescription Drugs First 
 For many Medicare beneficiaries, prescription medications are among their largest recurring healthcare expenses.
 That’s why reviewing a plan’s drug coverage should be one of the first steps in comparing options.
 Medicare Part D prescription drug plans and Medicare Advantage plans that include drug coverage maintain a list of covered medications known as a formulary .
 Those lists can change from year to year.
 A medication covered in 2026 might move to a more expensive tier in 2027. A plan could also change its requirements for prior authorization or other coverage restrictions.
 And some medications may no longer be covered.
 Don’t assume that because your prescriptions were covered this year, they’ll be covered the same way next year.
 The easiest place to begin is Medicare’s online Plan Finder at Medicare.gov/plan-compare .
 The tool allows you to enter your prescriptions, dosages, and preferred pharmacies, then compare estimated costs under different plans.
 Rather than focusing only on a $10 or $20 monthly premium difference, look at the estimated amount you’ll spend throughout the year.
 For 2027, the maximum Part D deductible increases to $700, up from $615 in 2026.
 The annual out-of-pocket threshold for covered Part D prescription drugs will be $2,400 in 2027, up from $2,100 this year.
 That protection is important, but it doesn’t include monthly premiums, noncovered medications, or all medical expenses.
 And not every patient will reach the threshold.
 Choosing a plan that covers your specific prescriptions at favorable costs still matters.
 Make Sure Your Pharmacy Is Preferred 
 Here’s something many Medicare beneficiaries overlook: The pharmacy you choose can affect how much you pay for exactly the same medication.
 Prescription drug plans generally establish pharmacy networks, and some designate certain locations as preferred pharmacies.
 Those preferred locations may offer lower copayments or coinsurance.
 A pharmacy that’s considered standard rather than preferred might charge more under the same insurance plan.
 That means a prescription could cost less at a participating pharmacy several miles away than at the drugstore across the street.
 The difference may be small for one medication, but it can add up for people taking several prescriptions every month.
 When comparing plans, enter the actual pharmacy you use into Medicare’s Plan Finder.
 Then consider checking another nearby pharmacy to see whether your estimated annual prescription costs change.
 Mail-order options may also be worth reviewing, particularly for medications taken regularly.
 However, convenience matters.
 A lower price may not be worth it if reaching the pharmacy creates transportation difficulties or makes it harder to get medications consistently.
 The goal is to find the best combination of affordability, access, and reliable service.
 Verify Your Doctors and Hospitals 
 Prescription expenses aren’t the only concern.
 For people enrolled in Medicare Advantage, provider networks can make a major difference in both access to care and out-of-pocket costs.
 Medicare Advantage plans generally use networks of participating physicians, specialists, hospitals, and other healthcare providers.
 Depending on the plan, seeing an out-of-network provider may cost more or have limited coverage.
 And those networks can change.
 A doctor who participated in your plan during 2026 may not necessarily participate in 2027.
 Before renewing or selecting a Medicare Advantage plan, make a list of your healthcare providers.
 Include your primary care physician, specialists, preferred hospital, and any facilities where you receive ongoing treatment.
 Then contact the insurance company or provider’s office to verify participation in the specific plan you’re considering for 2027.
 Don’t rely solely on an old printed directory or assume that a doctor’s participation in one plan means they accept every plan offered by the same insurer.
 A physician’s office may accept one Medicare Advantage product but not another.
 For someone receiving regular treatment, discovering a network change after January 1 can create serious inconvenience and unexpected expenses.
 Traditional Original Medicare works differently. Generally, beneficiaries can visit any doctor or hospital in the United States that accepts Medicare.
 Those with Medicare Supplement Insurance, commonly called Medigap, should also consider how that coverage affects their total costs.
 Don’t Forget Deductibles and Out-of-Pocket Limits 
 Even after checking prescriptions, pharmacies, and doctors, there’s another number worth understanding: the most you might have to pay if you need substantial medical care.
 Medicare Advantage plans have annual out-of-pocket limits for covered Medicare Part A and Part B services.
 Once you reach your plan’s applicable limit, the plan pays the covered costs for the remainder of the year.
 But those limits vary by plan, and they generally do not include monthly premiums or prescription drug spending.
 That means a plan with a lower premium may still cost you more if you need hospitalization, surgery, or frequent specialist visits.
 Original Medicare does not have a general annual out-of-pocket limit for Part A and Part B services unless you have supplemental coverage or other insurance that provides additional financial protection.
 Comparing the complete financial picture is especially important for people managing chronic health conditions.
 Help Is Available, and It Doesn’t Cost Anything 
 Medicare choices can be confusing, particularly when advertisements emphasize low premiums, dental benefits, or other attractive features.
 But you don’t have to sort through everything alone.
 Every state operates a State Health Insurance Assistance Program, commonly called SHIP.
 These programs provide free, unbiased Medicare counseling.
 In Virginia, the program is known as the Virginia Insurance Counseling and Assistance Program (VICAP) .
 VICAP counselors can help residents compare plans, understand prescription drug coverage, review out-of-pocket costs, and evaluate their Medicare options.
 They do not receive commissions for selling insurance plans.
 Virginia residents can call 1-800-552-3402 for assistance.
 Beneficiaries can also contact Medicare directly at 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227) or visit Medicare.gov .
 December 7 Is the Deadline 
 Medicare’s annual Open Enrollment Period runs from October 15 through December 7.
 For changes made during this period, new coverage generally takes effect January 1, 2027.
 The plan must receive your enrollment request by December 7. 
 Waiting until December 8 generally means the annual enrollment opportunity has closed.
 Some individuals may qualify for a Special Enrollment Period because of circumstances such as moving, losing certain coverage, or other qualifying events.
 People already enrolled in Medicare Advantage also have a separate enrollment period from January 1 through March 31, during which they can make certain changes.
 But those exceptions don’t replace the regular December 7 deadline for everyone.
 If you’re considering switching plans, it’s wise to decide before the final day.
 Compare What You’ll Actually Spend 
 A low monthly premium is appealing, particularly for retirees living on a fixed income.
 But saving $15 a month on premiums doesn’t help much if your prescriptions, office visits, or other healthcare expenses increase by hundreds of dollars.
 The best Medicare plan isn’t necessarily the one with the lowest advertised price.
 It’s the one that provides the coverage you need at a total cost you can manage.
 Before December 7, take a few minutes to check your medications, compare pharmacy prices, and verify your healthcare providers.
 Then look at the estimated expenses for the entire year.
 Your monthly premium is only the beginning of the calculation.
 What matters is what Medicare coverage will actually cost you to use.
